caption: Research Scope and Progression
rows: Current
⦅RO1: Trust-Centric Consent Model⦆

Develop a structured and evaluable representation of patient consent as a trust-aware authorisation object that explicitly connects identity, authority requirements, policy constraints, and authorisation evidence.
Current
RO2: Decentralised Identity and Authority Trust
Establish trustworthy participants using decentralised identifiers and verifiable credentials while explicitly separating identity authentication from authorisation authority.
Current
RO3: Trustworthy Multi-Party Authorisation
Establish collective trust by requiring multiple independently verified participants to satisfy predefined authorisation conditions before sensitive healthcare data access can be granted.
Current
⦅RO4: Policy- and Context-Aware Access Control⦆

Ensure that authorised access remains consistent with the purpose, policy, and healthcare data scope specified by the consent, preventing valid identities and approvals from being used to obtain data beyond the authorised constraints.
⟪Current⟫
RO5: Temporal and Lifecycle Trust
Extend the authorisation model with validity periods, expiration, revocation, and controlled consent-state transitions to support dynamic and lifecycle-aware trust evaluation.
⟪Current (empirical) / Next (formal)⟫
RO6: Formal Security Assurance and Empirical Validation

Formally define and analyse the security and authorisation properties of the proposed framework and empirically evaluate the complete HALAH implementation using representative healthcare data-sharing, negative, and adversarial scenarios.

caption: Comparison of Existing Research Approaches and the Proposed Framework
rows: Healthcare consent and privacy governance
Patient autonomy, informed consent, and controlled data sharing
Consent is treated as permission rather than an evaluable authorisation object
Blockchain-based data governance
Tamper-resistant records, distributed auditability, and transparency
Immutable records do not establish participant legitimacy, authority, or policy compliance
Decentralised identity and verifiable credentials
Self-controlled identity, verifiable attributes, and authentication
Identity and credential validity do not independently determine if access is authorised
Multi-party and decentralised governance
Collaborative participation and distributed verification or governance
Limited integration between collective approval thresholds, consent, and access decisions
Policy-based and healthcare access control
Fine-grained restriction based on attributes, risk, context, and constraints
Policy enforcement is separated from decentralised identity and multi-party consent
Trusted Computing and secure execution
Hardware-supported isolation, execution integrity, and attestation
Secure execution does not determine whether underlying authorisation conditions are sufficient
Proposed Framework
Integrated evaluation of consent, identity, authority, multi-party approval, and policy compliance
